sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Dumbbell Snatch is a powerful full-body compound movement derived from Olympic weightlifting, performed with a single dumbbell moving from the floor to an overhead locked-out position in one explosive motion.

It trains total-body power, coordination, and conditioning while also developing serious shoulder, back, and posterior chain strength.

The Dumbbell Snatch is a staple in athletic, CrossFit, and conditioning programs and offers a more accessible entry point to Olympic-style lifting than the barbell snatch.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Builds full-body explosive power
- Strengthens the shoulders, traps, and posterior chain
- Improves hip drive and triple extension mechanics
- Great conditioning tool for high-intensity workouts
- Develops core stability under overhead loads
- More accessible than the barbell snatch
- Improves grip strength and coordination
- Trains unilateral strength and anti-rotation stability

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Shoulders (all three deltoid heads), Glutes, Hamstrings, Quadriceps

Secondary: Trapezius, Latissimus Dorsi, Erector Spinae, Core, Forearms and Grip, Triceps, Calves

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Place a dumbbell on the ground between your feet.
2. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and back straight.
3. Reach down and grab the dumbbell with an overhand grip.
4. Keep your arm extended with your palm facing your body.
5. Keep your chest up, shoulders back, and core braced.
6. Position your hips back and shoulders slightly over the dumbbell.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Explosively drive through your heels and extend your legs and hips.
2. Simultaneously pull the dumbbell upwards in a swift, fluid motion.
3. Keep the dumbbell close to your body as it rises.
4. Shrug the shoulder and pull with the arm as the hips finish extending.
5. As the dumbbell rises, quickly rotate your hand, flipping your palm to face forward.
6. Continue pulling the weight overhead into a locked-out position.
7. Catch the weight with your arm fully extended, shoulder stable.
8. Lower the dumbbell back to the starting position with control and repeat.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Pulling with the arm too early instead of driving from the hips
- Allowing the dumbbell to drift away from the body
- Catching the weight with a soft or bent arm
- Rounding the lower back during the initial pull
- Using excessive back extension instead of hip drive
- Not fully locking out the arm overhead
- Losing control on the descent
- Rushing reps and sacrificing form

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Dumbbell (weight appropriate for the movement)
- Non-slip floor surface or lifting platform
- Open space above and around you for overhead movement
- Optional: Athletic shoes with good support
- Optional: Chalk or grip aid for heavier loads

sections.heading: Finding Your Position
sections.content:
1. Place the dumbbell on the ground between your feet.
2. Stand with feet about shoulder-width apart.
3. Hinge at the hips, soft bend in the knees.
4. Grab the dumbbell with an overhand grip, arm extended.
5. Keep the non-working arm relaxed or extended for balance.
6. Brace your core and set a neutral spine before lifting.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Shoulder-width, feet firmly planted.
2. Grip: Overhand grip on the dumbbell handle.
3. Hips: Loaded back, creating tension in the hamstrings.
4. Chest: Up, shoulders slightly over the dumbbell.
5. Core: Fully braced throughout the entire lift.
6. Arm: Straight on the pull, locked out at the top.
7. Breathing: Inhale and brace before the pull, exhale after lockout.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Kettlebell Snatch: Traditional unilateral ballistic movement
- Barbell Snatch: Olympic lift variation with a barbell
- Dumbbell Clean and Press: Slower two-movement alternative
- Dumbbell High Pull: Simplified version without the overhead finish
- Hang Dumbbell Snatch: Starting from the hip for beginners
- Dumbbell Swing: Hip hinge power movement without overhead catch

sections.heading: Snatch Variations
sections.content:
Dumbbell Snatch: Standard single-arm snatch from the floor
Hang Dumbbell Snatch: Starts from hip height for easier learning
Power Dumbbell Snatch: Catch with minimal knee bend
Alternating Dumbbell Snatch: Switches hands each rep
Double Dumbbell Snatch: Both arms simultaneously for advanced lifters
Single-Arm Dumbbell Squat Snatch: Full squat catch for maximum range

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Shoulder Mobility Issues: Work on thoracic and shoulder mobility first
Lower Back Pain: Start with hang snatches and reduce load
Knee Pain: Use a lighter load and focus on hip drive
Grip Issues: Use chalk or grip aids, or reduce reps
Beginner Level: Start with dumbbell high pulls and clean and press
No Dumbbell: Substitute with kettlebell snatch or barbell snatch
